summary: This experimental RFC, published on April 1, is humorous. It proposes hiding services from clients using the Domain Pseudonym System, a play on service discovery. It is satire.

eli5.summary: Instead of showing everything, this joke idea hides things so it is a game of hide and seek. It is an April Fools' joke.

questions: april fools rfc dns hide and seek
april fools hide and seek dns
subtitle: An April Fools' hide-and-seek game for DNS services.

tldr.problem: Service discovery protocols let clients find available services, but some services prefer to stay hidden from discovery.
tldr.mechanism: This April Fools' RFC proposes the Domain Pseudonym System (DPS), where services conceal themselves using fake names like 'gone-fishing' and play a hide-and-go-seek game with clients.
tldr.outcome: This is a humorous document published on April 1st, not a real protocol.

today: RFC 6593 is an Experimental RFC published on April 1, 2012, as a humorous April Fools' Day joke. It is not a real protocol and was never intended for actual implementation.

sections.title: Service Hiding Strategies
sections.content: RFC 6593 proposes the Domain Pseudonym System (DPS), a humorous protocol for services that want to remain undiscovered. A client attempting to find hidden services is called the seeker (or "it"), and the hidden service is the hider. Services conceal themselves by advertising under fake, funny, or nonsensical names such as "gone-fishing", "out-to-lunch", or "service-name-redacted" (shown as a black bar). Some services use silence-as-a-service: they simply do not respond.
sections.eli5: Services pretend to be things they are not. A music service might pretend to be a tax collection office. A service hiding silently just ignores requests.

sections.title: The Hide-and-Go-Seek Game
sections.content:
The RFC playfully describes a game where a seeker counts up to 50 (the Count to Live) before looking for services. Clients caught peeking early enter a timeout state, denied access to all services. Misbehaving clients may receive ICMP insult messages with codes like "LOSER", "DORK", and "TODAY IS SPECIAL", showing the humorous nature of the specification.

Services can also respond with hints: answering WARM or COLD to guesses about what service is available, with the seeker limited to 20 guesses before having to reset.
sections.eli5: The seeker closes their eyes and counts. If they peek too early, they are in trouble and cannot see any services. Services can give cold or warm hints to help the seeker guess what they are.

sections.title: Hidden Names and Disambiguity
sections.content: Services employ various sophisticated disguises: prime numbers, musical stars' names (like "Prince"), metasyntactic names (foo, bar, foobar), or complex word puzzles. Some services stay completely silent, implementing Silence-as-a-Service (SiaaS). The RFC tongue-in-cheek notes that the scoping service itself cannot be found because it is in hiding.
sections.eli5: Services pick silly names to hide. Some pretend to be nothing at all and just stay quiet.

sections.title: Echo Techniques
sections.content: A hider can repeat the service name that another service advertises, displayed in UTF-27 lowercase to suggest it is fading out. The hider may also echo the seeker's request straight back, confusing the seeker about whether the service is really there.
sections.eli5: A service can pretend to be a copy of another service or repeat what the seeker asks back to them.
